description: What each detector's finding means, why it matters, what to change, and when it is not a problem at all. The false-positive half is the part that saves a reviewer their afternoon.

detectors.title: Delegatecall to another contract
detectors.what_it_means: The contract executes code in another contract's context, using its own storage. The callee sees the caller's storage, and the caller's balance.
detectors.why_it_matters: If the address being delegated to can be influenced by an attacker, that code runs with the caller's authority and can take anything the contract holds. Even when the target is fixed, a delegatecall means the callee may write to the caller's storage in ways the caller does not expect.
detectors.how_to_fix: Never delegate to an address that a caller, an administrator, or any on-chain value can influence. Where a delegatecall is unavoidable, make the implementation self-contained: read the target from an immutable, admin-set value, and verify the target's code hash on deployment rather than trusting the address.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: The pattern is expected where the contract is an upgradeable proxy delegating to an immutable implementation, where the target address is fixed in immutable storage, or where the contract is itself a library called by a proxy and never holds funds. What matters is who controls the target, not the presence of the opcode.
detectors.references: SWC-105; Solidity documentation on delegatecall and proxies

detectors.title: tx.origin used where msg.sender belongs
detectors.what_it_means: The contract reads the address that signed the transaction rather than the address that called it.
detectors.why_it_matters: tx.origin is the outermost signer, so an intermediary contract can make the original signer look like the caller. A contract that authorizes on tx.origin lets any intermediary act on the signer's authority, which is how phishing contracts get the victim's authority.
detectors.how_to_fix: Authorize on msg.sender. If the contract genuinely needs to know the outermost signer, treat it as untrusted information and never let it satisfy an authorization check.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Reading tx.origin for logging, for analytics, or for a purely informational purpose is not a vulnerability. So is using it to identify the EOA behind a multisig for display. The finding matters when tx.origin is compared against an allowlist or used in an authorization decision.
detectors.references: SWC-115; Solidity documentation on msg.sender and tx.origin

detectors.title: SELFDESTRUCT reachable
detectors.what_it_means: The contract contains SELFDESTRUCT. Before Cancun, the contract can destroy itself and send its balance to an address it chooses. From Cancun onwards (EIP-6780) the contract's code survives: only the balance is forwarded, unless the contract was created in the same transaction, which the runtime bytecode cannot show.
detectors.why_it_matters: Before Cancun, a destroyed contract's code stays at its address but can never run again, so every function that moves funds becomes permanently unreachable. If the trigger is reachable by an attacker, the contract can be killed. From Cancun onwards the funds can still be swept away by whoever reaches the path, so the risk is the balance rather than the contract's functions -- which is why the finding narrows with the fork instead of repeating the older claim.
detectors.how_to_fix: Remove the SELFDESTRUCT from any path a user can reach. Where it exists for a migration, gate it behind an address that no user can become, and migrate funds rather than destroying the contract. On Cancun and later, replace it with an explicit withdrawal of the balance if the balance is what the path is about.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: A SELFDESTRUCT that is unreachable -- behind an impossible condition, or only callable by an immutable owner -- is not a live risk, though it is still worth removing. On Cancun and later the code is not destroyed at all, so a finding about the contract's code being unusable does not apply; the balance can still be swept, so a finding about the funds does.
detectors.references: SWC-106; EIP-6780 (the Cancun change to SELFDESTRUCT)

detectors.title: External call before the state is written
detectors.what_it_means: The contract calls out to another address before recording the state change that the call is supposed to cause.
detectors.why_it_matters: If the called address can call back into this contract, it can re-enter it while the state still says the action has not happened. The classic consequence is a balance that is read twice: once before the update and once after.
detectors.how_to_fix: Follow the checks-effects-interactions pattern: validate the inputs, write the state, and only then make the external call. Where a call must precede the write, guard the entry point with a re-entrancy lock and make sure the state it relies on is already final.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: The pattern is expected where the call is to a trusted, immutable address that cannot call back -- a well-known token, for instance. It is also expected where the state written afterwards is not relied upon by the callee. What matters is whether the callee can re-enter, not the ordering alone.
detectors.references: SWC-107; Solidity documentation on checks-effects-interactions

detectors.title: Stack depth goes negative
detectors.what_it_means: A linear simulation of the code reaches a stack position below zero: the code reads more values than it has.
detectors.why_it_matters: This is not a vulnerability by itself; it is a sign that the disassembly and the runtime's stack do not agree. Either the analysis has mis-decoded the bytecode, or the code depends on stack state that the analysis cannot model -- usually because a jump destination was resolved incorrectly.
detectors.how_to_fix: Treat this as an analysis fault, not a contract fault. Check that the fork and the bytecode match the deployed contract, and that the disassembler resolved every jump. Only then consider whether the contract itself is malformed.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Most occurrences are artifacts: a jump into the middle of a PUSH immediate, or an unresolved dynamic jump. The finding is a prompt to check the analysis, and on its own it says nothing about the contract's safety.
detectors.references: The CyberStratum correspondence prover; the scan's fork_resolution artefact

detectors.title: A jump destination could not be resolved
detectors.what_it_means: The control-flow graph could not decide where a dynamic jump lands, so the code after it could not be analysed.
detectors.why_it_matters: An unresolved jump is a blind spot. Anything the code does after that jump is invisible to the analysis, and a finding that is not there is not the same as a finding that is absent.
detectors.how_to_fix: Treat the scan as partial. The rules still ran over everything that was resolved, but the result does not cover the whole contract. Resolve the jump -- often by looking at the jump table the contract builds at run time -- before relying on the result.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Some contracts compute their jump targets at run time from a table, and the analysis cannot follow them without running the code. Those contracts are genuinely only partly analysable, and the honest answer is to say so rather than to report the scan as complete.
detectors.references: The scan's CFG artefact; the scan status (partial rather than completed)

detectors.title: Inline assembly bypasses the compiler's checks
detectors.what_it_means: The contract contains an `assembly` block, where Solidity's own safety rules do not apply: the compiler does not check arithmetic, memory bounds, or storage layout inside it.
detectors.why_it_matters: Everything the compiler would have refused to compile is now the author's responsibility. A block that writes past the intended memory range, or that divides without checking for zero, behaves exactly as written -- and the reviewer has to read the opcodes to know that. Assembly is also where the classic proxy pattern lives, so a block often holds the most security-sensitive code in the contract.
detectors.how_to_fix: Use assembly only where Solidity cannot express the operation, and keep the block as small as possible. Inside a block, check the arithmetic and the memory bounds yourself: verify the free memory pointer before writing, check the divisor, and use the `verbatim` form only when you can state why the compiler's output is wrong. Where a block exists to save gas, measure the saving first; most blocks cost more in review time than they save.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Assembly is expected in a proxy's fallback, in a gas-optimised hot path that has been reviewed, in an immutable-variable accessor, and in contracts that implement their own storage layout deliberately. What matters is what the block does and who controls its inputs, not that assembly is present.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: Inline Assembly; SWC-127

detectors.title: The compiler version in use has known problems
detectors.what_it_means: The contract declares or is built with a Solidity compiler version that Slither knows to be affected by a bug, or that predates a language change worth knowing about.
detectors.why_it_matters: Some compiler versions miscompile code that looks correct in the source. The failure is in the binary, so reviewing the source will not reveal it, and the deployed bytecode will not match what the author believed they deployed. The version is also the anchor for every other tool's assumption about the code, including this product's.
detectors.how_to_fix: Recompile with a current, patched release of the compiler, pin the exact version in the build rather than a floating range, and rebuild and redeploy if the deployed bytecode was produced by a version with a known bug. Record the compiler version in the deployment metadata so the artefact can be traced back to the tool that made it.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: The finding is about the compiler, not the contract's logic. A contract compiled with an old version that has no known miscompilation is a hygiene issue rather than a vulnerability, and a contract that was never recompiled after the fix may still be safe. Read the advisory before treating it as exploitable.
detectors.references: Solidity security advisories and bug list; Slither documentation: solc version detector

detectors.title: A variable marked immutable is never changed
detectors.what_it_means: The contract declares a state variable `immutable` but never assigns it a different value after construction, so it could be a `constant` instead.
detectors.why_it_matters: An immutable variable is written into the deployed bytecode, which costs a little gas on every read and enlarges the contract. It is a code-hygiene finding rather than a vulnerability: the risk is that a reader assumes an immutable can be changed by an owner, or that a variable marked immutable is actually a constant and cannot be set at construction.
detectors.how_to_fix: Declare the variable `constant` if it is known at compile time, or `immutable` if it is known only at construction and read from the constructor's argument. Then read the constructor to check that the value is set exactly once.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: An immutable that is written in the constructor and never again is the correct use of the keyword; Slither reports the pattern where the value could equally be a compile-time constant. Where the value is set through a proxy's initializer, the variable is not immutable at all.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: Immutable variables and constants

detectors.title: Ether sent to this contract cannot be recovered
detectors.what_it_means: The contract can receive Ether -- through a `receive` or `payable` fallback, or because it is the target of a plain transfer -- but it has no function that sends Ether out of its own balance.
detectors.why_it_matters: Any Ether that reaches the contract is stuck there for ever: the users who sent it cannot get it back, and the balance sits in the contract while doing nothing. In a contract that was meant to hold funds temporarily, or one that was upgraded without a withdrawal path, this is a direct loss of money.
detectors.how_to_fix: Add a function that lets the intended party withdraw the balance, guarded by the same access control as the rest of the contract, and make the amount and recipient explicit. If the contract should not hold Ether at all, remove the `payable` fallback so an accidental transfer reverts instead of succeeding.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: The contract may be one half of a pair, where the counterparty holds the withdrawal path, or it may forward Ether immediately in the fallback. Some Ether may also be recoverable by the selfdestruct of another contract. The finding matters where the contract keeps a balance of its own with no way out.
detectors.references: SWC-107; Solidity documentation: receive and fallback functions

detectors.title: A numeric literal is too long to be exact
detectors.what_it_means: The contract contains a decimal literal with more than fifteen significant digits.
detectors.why_it_matters: Beyond fifteen digits the value no longer fits exactly in the 80-bit mantissa of the EVM's fixed-point arithmetic, and the compiler silently rounds it. A constant that was meant to be exact -- a token's maximum supply, a basis-point denominator, a fixed rate -- ends up slightly different from what the author wrote, and the difference compounds through every calculation that uses it.
detectors.how_to_fix: Write the value in a smaller unit where it fits exactly, split it into a numerator and a denominator that are each representable, or express it as a rational computation instead of a literal. Where the value is a rate, state it in the unit the contract actually uses.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: A literal that is deliberately rounded -- a display constant, a wei-denominated dust amount -- is harmless. The finding is about the loss of exactness, not about the number itself, so a value whose rounding is intended is not a defect.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: Rational number literals; SWC-131

detectors.title: Code that can never run
detectors.what_it_means: The contract contains a variable, a function, or a branch that is never used, or code that follows an unconditional return or revert.
detectors.why_it_matters: Dead code is usually the remains of a removed feature, and it keeps the contract's surface area larger than it looks. It also misleads the reader: a function nobody calls may look like part of the contract's public behaviour, and an unreachable branch may be the place where a check was meant to be. Unreachable code is also a place where a compiler bug can hide.
detectors.how_to_fix: Delete the unused code. If the code documents an intent -- a check that should be reinstated, a future switch -- put that intent in a comment and in the tests rather than in unreachable statements.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Functions reached through a low-level call, a delegatecall, a proxy dispatch, or a hook invoked by another contract are not dead. A modifier's code can be used through a function that inherits it, and a variable read only in assembly is not dead.
detectors.references: Slither documentation: dead code detector

detectors.title: A low-level call whose result is not checked
detectors.what_it_means: The contract calls another address with `address.call`, `address.send`, or `address.transfer` -- the low-level interfaces -- where the outcome is not examined, or where the call forwards all remaining gas.
detectors.why_it_matters: A low-level call that fails returns false rather than reverting, so a contract that does not check the result will carry on as if the call had succeeded: a payment that never arrived, a state change that never happened. A call that forwards all gas also lets the callee consume everything the caller had, which is how a loop of calls becomes a denial of service.
detectors.how_to_fix: Check the returned boolean and revert when it is false, or use a high-level call to an interface, which reverts on failure. When forwarding gas is not needed, cap it with the 2300-gas stipend of `transfer`. Handle the failure explicitly rather than ignoring it.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: The call may deliberately ignore the result -- a best-effort call, a payout where the caller has already been debited -- in which case the pattern should be commented so the next reader does not have to work it out. A call whose failure is checked on the next line is not this finding.
detectors.references: SWC-104; Solidity documentation: Low-level calls

detectors.title: The return value of an internal function is never used
detectors.what_it_means: An internal function returns a value that its caller discards, or a function's declared return type does not match what it actually returns.
detectors.why_it_matters: A discarded return value usually means the function was meant to report something -- a balance, a result, an error -- and the caller was written without it. The information is computed and thrown away, so a check that was supposed to happen never does. Where the declared and the actual return type differ, the value the caller reads is not the value the function computed.
detectors.how_to_fix: Either use the returned value where it is needed, or change the function so that it does not return one. Where the function is meant to report a failure, make it revert rather than return a value nobody reads.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Some functions return a value for their own callers in an interface, or the value is read in assembly. A function whose return value is only used in a test is not dead in the compiler's sense, but the pattern still deserves a look.
detectors.references: Slither documentation: incorrect return detector

detectors.title: An address in an event is not indexed
detectors.what_it_means: The contract emits an event that carries an address parameter which is not marked `indexed`, so the address is stored in the log's data rather than in its topics.
detectors.why_it_matters: An indexed parameter can be filtered on by a node or an indexer without reading the log's data, which is what makes an event usable for tracking. An address that is not indexed has to be read out of the data by every consumer, and -- for a log with three indexed parameters already -- the change may not be possible at all.
detectors.how_to_fix: Mark the address `indexed` where the event is meant to be queried by it. Where it cannot be indexed because the event already has three indexed parameters, consider whether a second event, or a hash of the address, would serve the consumers better.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: An event that exists only for a human reading in a block explorer has no need for indexing. An address that is deliberately in the data -- so that the log's data is self-contained -- is a reasonable design.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: Events; Solidity security considerations: events

detectors.title: The result of an external call is not used
detectors.what_it_means: The contract calls another contract and ignores what the call returned.
detectors.why_it_matters: A call to an external contract can fail, return a false, or return a value that carries the outcome -- a boolean success, an amount actually received, a token balance after the transfer. Discarding it means the contract proceeds on the assumption that the operation worked, so a failed transfer looks like a successful one, and the accounting drifts away from reality.
detectors.how_to_fix: Capture the returned value and check it: revert when the call failed, or account for the amount that was actually received rather than the amount that was sent. Where the call is a token transfer, read the balance before and after, or use a library that checks the return value for you.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: The call may be one whose outcome the contract handles by other means -- a `safeTransfer` that reverts on failure already, or a call whose effect is observed through the contract's own state. A deliberate best-effort call should say so in a comment.
detectors.references: Solidity security considerations: checks for return values; SWC-104

detectors.title: Division happens before multiplication
detectors.what_it_means: The contract computes `a / b * c`, or `a / b % c`, where the intended order is `a * c / b`.
detectors.why_it_matters: Integer division truncates, so dividing first throws away the remainder before the multiplication can use it. The result is systematically smaller than the mathematically correct one, and the size of the error grows with the size of the numbers -- which is exactly what happens as a pool fills or an amount grows. In a share or fee calculation the error is paid by one side and pocketed by the other.
detectors.how_to_fix: Multiply before dividing: rewrite the expression as `a * c / b`. Where the multiplication could overflow, use a wider intermediate type or a full-precision library, and check the result against a test with large values.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Where the division is exact -- the divisor divides the numerator -- the two orders give the same answer, and the finding is harmless. The same applies when the truncated remainder is intended, as in an integer pixel or tick division.
detectors.references: Solidity security considerations: integer overflow and underflow; SWC-101

detectors.title: An external call inside a loop
detectors.what_it_means: The contract makes an external call to another address while iterating over a collection.
detectors.why_it_matters: The number of iterations is usually controlled by data that grows -- the number of holders, the number of assets, the length of a queue -- and every iteration can cost an arbitrary amount of gas because the callee is another contract. When the total exceeds the block's gas limit the transaction cannot be included at all, and a function that can be made to run out of gas can be used to freeze the contract's own operations.
detectors.how_to_fix: Bound the loop by a value the protocol accepts, such as a maximum number of entries per call, and let the caller process the rest in separate transactions. Prefer pull payments over push payments, so that one recipient's failure cannot stop the others. Where the call must happen, cap the gas it may use.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: A loop over a fixed, small array -- a constant-length list of assets, for instance -- cannot be grown by an attacker and is not a denial of service. A loop that the caller can only fill with entries it created itself, and that can be emptied by a per-user claim, is the pattern that keeps the risk away.
detectors.references: Solidity security considerations: Loops; SWC-107

detectors.title: Ether can be sent to an address the caller chooses
detectors.what_it_means: The contract sends its Ether balance, or part of it, to an address that comes from the caller's arguments.
detectors.why_it_matters: If the contract keeps a balance that belongs to the protocol -- a fee, a reward, a withdrawal queue -- then a caller who can name the recipient can take that balance for themselves. The balance does not have to be large at the moment of the call: it can be built up over time, and the call that drains it can happen on the day the balance is largest.
detectors.how_to_fix: Send the Ether only to an address the protocol already trusts: a beneficiary recorded when the deposit was made, an owner set at construction, or an address validated against a whitelist. Where the recipient is genuinely chosen by the caller, make sure the amount sent is only what that caller deposited.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: A withdrawal to a caller-supplied address is the intended behaviour of a vault that tracks each depositor's own balance -- the finding is only about the contract sending more than the caller is owed. A payout that sends exactly the recorded share to the recorded recipient is not this finding.
detectors.references: SWC-105; Solidity security considerations: withdrawals

detectors.title: A name does not follow the project's convention
detectors.what_it_means: A variable, constant, function, or argument is named differently from the convention the rest of the codebase uses.
detectors.why_it_matters: Names are how a reviewer reads a contract quickly. A constant that looks like a variable, or a function whose name hides what it does, costs time on every review and every audit -- and a mismatch between a name and a behaviour is often where a real bug hides.
detectors.how_to_fix: Rename the identifier to the convention the project uses: `camelCase` for variables, functions, and arguments, `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` for constants, and a capitalised first letter for structs, events, and errors. Renaming an external or public function changes the contract's interface, so treat it as an interface change and coordinate it.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: The finding is about consistency, not correctness: it says nothing about whether the code is safe. A project with its own documented convention -- or a naming that is deliberate, such as a leading underscore for an internal name -- is not a problem.
detectors.references: Solidity style guide; Slither documentation: naming convention detector

detectors.title: An overridden function does not keep its modifier
detectors.what_it_means: A function overrides a function of a base contract or an interface, and the base declares a modifier -- typically an access-control or a re-entrancy guard -- that the override does not repeat.
detectors.why_it_matters: A modifier is part of a function's contract with its callers: it is what says who may call it and under what conditions. When an override drops the modifier, the function is callable by anyone, or callable re-entrantly, exactly as the base contract's author intended to prevent. The base contract's protection is now a suggestion.
detectors.how_to_fix: Copy the modifier onto the override, so the guarantee the base contract offers is kept. Where the override deliberately relaxes it, say so in a comment that explains why, and check that nothing else relies on the guarantee.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Where the base function is `virtual` and its modifier is documentation rather than enforcement, the override may be safe. A modifier that the override calls through another internal function -- an `internalCall` that applies it -- is not a missing modifier.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: Function overriding; Solidity security considerations: modifiers

detectors.title: A contract does not implement everything it inherits
detectors.what_it_means: A contract inherits from a base contract or an interface, but at least one of the inherited functions is not implemented.
detectors.why_it_matters: Such a contract cannot be deployed -- the compiler rejects it -- which means either the deployment is blocked or the contract that is deployed is not the one that was reviewed. Where the missing function is only noticed at deployment time, the review has already been wasted, and the fallback is usually to remove the inheritance, which removes the guarantees the base contract provided.
detectors.how_to_fix: Implement the missing function, or remove the inheritance if the contract is not meant to be that kind of contract. Where the base is an interface, implement every function it declares; where it is a shared base, check that the inherited state and modifiers are wanted.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: The contract may be an abstract base that is never deployed on its own -- in that case the finding is a deployment-time check rather than a defect. Check whether the contract is ever the direct target of a deployment.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: Abstract contracts and interfaces; Slither documentation: missing inheritance detector

detectors.title: The contract depends on the block timestamp
detectors.what_it_means: The contract reads `block.timestamp` -- directly or through `now` -- and uses it in a decision.
detectors.why_it_matters: A block's timestamp is chosen by its producer within a small window, so a validator can influence it by a few seconds. Where the timestamp decides a winner of a race, a random number, a deadline that must not be crossed, or the order of two competing transactions, that influence is enough to change the outcome. The value is also the only source of on-chain time, so a contract with no other time source has nothing to compare it against.
detectors.how_to_fix: Where the timestamp only enforces a minimum delay -- a vesting schedule, a cooldown -- a small manipulation is harmless, and the finding can be accepted. Where it selects a winner or a random outcome, use a source the producer cannot steer: a commit-and-reveal scheme, a verifiable random function, or an oracle that aggregates several blocks.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Using the timestamp for a delay, an expiry, or a reporting window is normal and safe, because the producer's few seconds of freedom cannot be used to profit. The finding matters where the exact second decides something worth money.
detectors.references: SWC-116; Solidity security considerations: block timestamp dependence

detectors.title: An event reports a value that may no longer be true
detectors.what_it_means: The contract emits an event whose parameter is read from storage, after an external call has already been made in the same transaction.
detectors.why_it_matters: The event is what an indexer and a user read to know what happened. If the value was changed -- by the callee, through a re-entrant call -- the event reports a number that no longer matches the contract's state, so the record and the truth disagree. Off-chain systems that reconstruct state from events then hold a state the chain does not have.
detectors.how_to_fix: Read the value before making the external call and emit it from the local copy, or re-read the value after the call and emit that. Where the contract's state is the authority, emit the state rather than a value captured earlier.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Where the external call cannot change the contract's state -- a call to a view function, or one to a contract that cannot re-enter -- the value is the same before and after, and the finding does not apply.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: Events; Slither documentation: events access detector

detectors.title: Tokens can be sent to an address the caller chooses
detectors.what_it_means: The contract transfers its ERC-20 token balance, or part of it, to an address taken from the caller's arguments.
detectors.why_it_matters: If the contract holds tokens that belong to the protocol -- fees collected, rewards owed to users, a treasury -- then a caller who can name the recipient can take them. The tokens are often worth more than the contract's Ether balance, and the balance may sit idle for a long time before anyone tries to take it.
detectors.how_to_fix: Send tokens only to an address the protocol already trusts: the recipient recorded when the deposit was made, a beneficiary set at construction, or an address on a whitelist. Where the recipient is genuinely the caller's choice, send only what that caller is owed.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: A withdrawal that pays the caller exactly their own recorded balance is the intended behaviour of a vault, not a defect. The finding is about the contract being able to pay more than the caller is entitled to.
detectors.references: SWC-105; Solidity security considerations: withdrawals

detectors.title: A division or modulo without a zero check
detectors.what_it_means: The contract divides or takes a modulo by a value that is not checked to be non-zero.
detectors.why_it_matters: Division by zero in the EVM reverts the transaction, so the caller's transaction fails and any state it had already written is rolled back. Where the denominator comes from a caller's argument, or from a ratio the contract computes, an attacker can choose a zero and make the function unusable; where it comes from a balance that can be emptied, the same failure arrives on its own.
detectors.how_to_fix: Check the denominator before using it and revert with a clear message when it is zero. Where the divisor is a user-supplied number, reject zero at the entry point. Where a ratio is computed from two balances, guard the divisor and the multiplication that goes with it.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: A denominator that the contract has already proved non-zero -- a constant, or a value checked earlier in the same function -- needs no second check. Slither reports the pattern, not the proof; read the function before deciding.
detectors.references: Solidity security considerations: Integer overflow and underflow; SWC-101

detectors.title: An exponent is not a constant
detectors.what_it_means: The contract raises a number to a power whose exponent is not a compile-time constant.
detectors.why_it_matters: An exponentiation whose exponent is a variable costs far more gas than a constant one, and the cost grows with the exponent: an attacker who can influence the exponent can make the transaction exceed the block gas limit, which makes the function unusable. The result is also easy to get wrong, because the base and the exponent are easy to transpose.
detectors.how_to_fix: Use a constant exponent, or replace the exponentiation with repeated multiplication that the compiler can unroll. Where the exponent must vary, bound it explicitly and reject anything above the bound before the computation runs.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: An exponent that is a constant in practice -- a literal, or a variable the contract has already constrained to a small fixed set -- is fine, and the gas cost is bounded. Slither reports the pattern; the bound may already be in place.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: Operators; Slither documentation: incorrect exponentiation detector

detectors.title: A function is too branchy to review
detectors.what_it_means: A function's cyclomatic complexity -- the number of independent paths through it -- exceeds the threshold the analysis was run with.
detectors.why_it_matters: Complexity is a proxy for how many things can go wrong. A function with many branches is where a missing check hides, because no reader holds all the paths at once. It is also where audits spend their time, and where the parts that are never exercised by the tests live.
detectors.how_to_fix: Split the function into smaller ones, each with one job, and move the validation into a modifier or an internal helper that can be tested on its own. Where the branches are a chain of conditions, model them as a lookup or as a state machine rather than as nested conditionals.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: The threshold is a rule of thumb, not a defect: a function can be complex and correct, or simple and wrong. Read it. Where the branches are mutually exclusive and short -- a type dispatch -- the complexity number overstates the difficulty.
detectors.references: Slither documentation: cyclomatic complexity detector

detectors.title: The compiler version is not pinned
detectors.what_it_means: The contract declares a Solidity version with a floating range -- `pragma solidity ^0.8.0` -- rather than an exact version.
detectors.why_it_matters: A range means the build is not reproducible: the same source compiles into different bytecode on a different day, and a compiler release inside the range can change the code that is deployed. Two deployments of the same source are then different contracts, with different bytecode hashes and different behaviour, while looking identical in the repository.
detectors.how_to_fix: Pin the exact compiler version in the build, and record it in the contract's metadata so the deployed artefact can be traced back to the tool that produced it. Where the range has to stay wide, pin the version that the deployment pipeline actually uses and verify the deployed bytecode against it.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: A library that must compile with several compiler versions, or a repository whose build pins the version elsewhere -- a lockfile, a CI image -- is reproducible in practice. The finding is about where the pin is written, so check the whole build before acting on it.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: Pragmas; SWC-108

detectors.title: The outcome depends on the order of transactions
detectors.what_it_means: The contract's behaviour changes depending on which transaction is mined first -- usually because it reads a value that another transaction can change in between, such as a price, a balance, or a stake.
detectors.why_it_matters: When two transactions conflict and the order decides which one wins, the earlier sender is at the mercy of the later one: a liquidator who is a moment too late loses their position, a buyer pays a different price, and a participant can be made to lose by watching the mempool. An attacker who can pay a little more for gas can take the favourable order and leave the other side with the loss.
detectors.how_to_fix: Design the contract so that the order does not matter: make the decision from a value that only the transaction itself supplies, use a commit-and-reveal scheme where the committed value is fixed before the revealing transaction is sent, or take the disputed value from an oracle that aggregates over several blocks.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Order dependence is not a defect where the contract says explicitly which order it expects and compensates the loser -- a liquidator paid a penalty, a bidder whose bid was overtaken refunded -- or where the value being read cannot change between the two transactions.
detectors.references: SWC-114; Solidity security considerations: transaction order dependence

detectors.title: A state variable can be written without permission
detectors.what_it_means: The contract declares a state variable that is publicly writable, or a setter that does not check who is calling it, so anybody can set it.
detectors.why_it_matters: A variable that anyone can set is a variable the protocol does not control. If it holds an address, a price, a fee, or a limit, then an attacker writes the value that suits them and the contract behaves as they intended. The rest of the contract is then correct code following the wrong input.
detectors.how_to_fix: Make the variable `private` or `internal` and expose a function that checks the caller's role before writing it, or make it `public` only when the protocol genuinely intends the value to be set by anybody. Where the value must be set by an administrator, name the role explicitly.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: A variable that is intentionally open -- a fee that the protocol wants the market to set, a flag that anyone may raise -- is not a defect. A variable written only by a constructor or an initialiser is not publicly writable at runtime.
detectors.references: SWC-105; Solidity documentation: State variables and visibility

detectors.title: A re-entrant call forwards all the gas
detectors.what_it_means: The contract makes a call that can call back into it, and that call forwards all the remaining gas to the callee.
detectors.why_it_matters: The callee decides how much gas to use. When the whole remainder goes with it, the re-entrant path can be driven into an out-of-gas, and the failure lands in the middle of the caller's own work: state the caller had already written is then either rolled back with the whole transaction, or -- where the caller catches the failure -- left in place while the inner frame's changes were undone. The two halves of the contract then disagree about what happened.
detectors.how_to_fix: Forward a bounded amount of gas rather than the remainder, so the re-entrant path is given the budget it was written for, and treat a callee that runs out of gas as a handled failure rather than as an event to ignore. Where the callee is trusted and known not to call back, forwarding everything is harmless and the finding can be accepted.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: The finding is about the combination: a re-entrant call that also forwards all the gas. A call to a contract that cannot call back is not a re-entrancy, and forwarding all the gas to a trusted callee that only reads state is not a problem.
detectors.references: Solidity security considerations: re-entrancy; Slither documentation: reentrancy with unlimited gas detector
